sentences.text: Participant A stated that the data processing is fine but they do not want to build the GUI for it.
Participant C agreed to build the GUI.
Participant A explained that the current architecture uses two separate classes: one for speakers and one for meetings, where information about both is contained within each object
Participant A noted that the speaker class contains information on who participated in meetings, the amount they spoke, and averages.
Participant A stated that all data is stored as object files.
Participant A explained that the data structures currently use hash tables for meetings containing fields for percent talk, percent noise, and percent participation, with links to
Participant A proposed that the data could be returned either as a hash table or as a vector/array of strings.
Participant A mentioned that the data is pre-processed offline and stored as object files which are much smaller than raw files.
Participant A stated that each meeting has one object.
Participant A proposed that methods should be created to return specific numbers (e.g., talking time) one at a time to populate windows.
Participant A suggested that the box should be populated by the speaker present, though they acknowledged it could be populated by the highlighted speaker.
Participant C proposed that the system could be used to iterate through topics and meetings to find the most interesting speakers.
Participant A agreed to leave in methods that return one number at a time.
Participant C asked if the system could include the topic spoken about in the output.
Participant A agreed that adding the topic would be easy.
Participant C noted that the current system allows right-clicking on a topic window to open a list of all meetings containing that topic.
Participant A suggested that the system could perform a search over the loaded meeting objects to find participants and topics.
Participant A mentioned that there are default topics available.
Participant A stated that global statistics come straight from the pre-processed data.
Participant A mentioned that the speaker class knows about all the data stuff and the meeting class knows about that stuff.
Participant A stated they have not yet completed the tasks mentioned by Participant C, estimating they would not be difficult.
Participant A explained that if Participant C were to work on the GUI before Participant A finished the classes, the object serial numbers would change, preventing re-loading of a
Participant A requested that Participant C wait until the current work is finished before starting on the GUI to avoid objects becoming out of sync.
Participant A indicated that Participant C could proceed with creating the picture and text box components without waiting, as these do not depend on the current unfinished work.
Participant A stated that the data is currently stored on their home directory and has not yet been globalized.
Participant B confirmed they have a copy of the file in their own directory and will create one with a specific change to load the correct search file.
Participant B mentioned they intend to update their copy of the file after making the necessary change.
Participant B described their current work as improving result presentation, specifically by wiring in topics and summaries.
Participant C explained that the text area already has defined highlights for user, selection, and time topics.
Participant C provided a code example suggesting setting highlights on a text area object (e.g., `area dot set highlights`).
Participant C mentioned they are working on pop-up windows for speaker characterization.
Participant C explained that pop-up windows must be pre-initialized in memory because there may be ten speakers requiring different meeting windows.
Participant C proposed a start screen option that displays a welcome message for the meeting browser.
Participant A suggested a start screen option featuring speech, music, and drum rolls.
Participant A suggested a start screen option featuring a switchboard with buttons to load a meeting, perform a search, or load something else.
Participant C noted that the current interface uses a dropdown menu controlled by the dialogue class.
Participant C proposed two options for the start screen: either load a specific meeting or perform a global search to find a meeting.
Participant A explained that the search engine requires an observation (nom object) to function and cannot perform searches without it.
Participant B agreed that a check should be implemented to force the user to load a meeting before attempting a search.
Participant A explained that the search engine class only has one search method, which requires an observation to start.
Participant B noted that loading the entire corpus for a global search could be time-consuming if ten documents are returned.
Participant A stated that loading ten different search engines simultaneously would crash the system.
Participant A stated that the current loading speed is not too slow and should not be considered a problem.
Participant B noted that the system typically loads slowly for the first time and mentioned a workaround of loading, testing, and shutting down to reload.
Participant B suggested that if the loading time is not long each time, the situation would be acceptable.
Participant C proposed a search strategy involving a global search for meeting names first, followed by narrowing down to specific meetings.
Participant A suggested making search strings as long as possible to limit search occurrences to when they are actually needed.
Participant B agreed that avoiding extra loading time is important for users.
Participant B suggested users could check off specific items they want to review.
Participant A raised the need for better names for the meetings.
Participant B indicated that better names could be created by extracting strings from the text.
Participant C mentioned that some papers contain names such as 'better understanding' or similar long names.
Participant B confirmed that the names include the working group they are part of.
Participant A decided to use the names found in the papers.
Participant A expressed a wish to see meetings related to 'even better understanding'.
Participant C confirmed they had already added the 'even better understanding' name to the list.
Participant C discussed the startup screen and libraries window.
Participant A asked about the document frequencies (DFs) for each word in the corpus.
Participant B questioned whether the frequencies were actually needed.
Participant A confirmed that the frequencies are needed to perform topic labeling.
Participant B mentioned that someone named Steve was trying to get a tool working on Friday, which had previously included standard stuff but was not working properly.
Participant A asked if the system could perform search without using term frequency (TF) or inverse document frequency (IDF).
Participant B admitted they did not know if the system could do better without TF/IDF.
Participant A explained that TF is the amount a word occurs in each document, IDF is the amount it occurs generally, and the combination (TF-IDF) indicates how informative a term's
Participant A clarified that TF-IDF stands for Term Frequency Inverse Document Frequency.
Participant A mentioned they have a Java class that performs TF-IDF calculations, though they were unsure if it would work with the current data.
Participant C expressed that having the ability to test the tool on users would be really handy.
Participant C noted that without testing against hand-annotated segmented tools, they cannot compare results effectively.
Participant A explained that keyword search could function as topic search, searching for keywords while the user specifies topics.
Participant C agreed that calculating keyword frequencies based on whole occurrences in the corpus would be easier than calculating them per topic.
Participant A stated that searching without TF-IDF allows for search but prevents ranking results.
Participant C agreed that ranking results by the amount of occurrence would be a nice extra feature.
Participant C suggested adding a longer meeting name and a list of users who spoke to the meeting to the startup screen.
Participant B agreed that the list of users would likely be the same for the same group.
Participant A suggested placing this information on the startup screen to give users a general idea of available meetings.
Participant B proposed that users could either search for specific meetings or browse through them.
Participant C agreed that users might want to look at specific meetings where particular speakers spoke.
Participant B suggested that the startup screen could include options to browse by meeting, speaker, or working group.
Participant C disagreed with the need for detailed filtering options like browsing by speaker or working group.
Participant C argued that once a user loads a meeting, they can browse through it sufficiently without needing pre-filtered lists.
Participant B suggested that the system could default to showing meetings relevant to the user's specific working group based on their previous activity.
Participant C questioned how the system would know which working group a user belongs to.
Participant B proposed using a user model to determine the user's working group.
Participant A suggested implementing a 'favourites' feature instead of automatic defaults.
Participant C agreed that users do not come back daily to perform the same browsing tasks.
Participant B noted that users might want to see what has changed since their last visit.
Participant B proposed that the startup screen could include search options, browse options, and links to evaluation tasks.
Participant A agreed that having search buttons on the startup screen would be useful.
Participant C stated they did not want to include explanatory help text on the startup screen.
Participant B suggested that the startup screen should guide users to commonly used tasks or allow them to exit, similar to other programs.
Participant C agreed that the main function of the startup screen should be to view a meeting or search for one.
Participant A proposed a design where the startup screen displays a single window with a search box, a 'go' button, and a dropdown menu for specific meetings.
Participant A suggested that the search window could contain a dropdown menu with a 'go' button to take the user directly to a meeting.
Participant C agreed with the proposal to have a single window containing all search functionality and a 'go' button.
Participant C expressed uncertainty about how to display all available information (name, longer name, speakers, users) in the startup screen.
Participant B noted that the system currently does not have user names, only codes like 'ami eleven'.
Participant A agreed that the codes are nonsense and should not be typed by the user.
Participant B confirmed that a dropdown menu is preferred for selecting a specific speaker rather than typing codes.
Participant A suggested that if a user wants to look at one specific meeting, they can simply click on it.
Participant C proposed an extended list of meetings with longer names and participants, potentially using a tool-tip mechanism when hovering over items.
Participant C suggested using a tool-tip to display information when the mouse hovers over a meeting item.
Participant A agreed to implement the tool-tip feature.
Participant C proposed a meeting time of 3:00 PM on Friday.
Participant A suggested that 3:00 PM might be problematic because they would not be available at 5:00 PM or 6:00 PM.
Participant C agreed to schedule the meeting for 3:00 PM pending any issues arising.
Participant C confirmed that Pernilla does not collect meeting summaries because she is not present.
Participant C stated they collect meeting summaries.
The group discussed progress on speaker characterisation and topic labelling with keywords.
Participant B expressed uncertainty about whether the search results should be ranked, noting that Michael had no additional input on this.
Participant B argued that ranking search results independently for specific documents would complicate things without providing significant benefit.
Participant C argued that ranking would provide the most relevant results by distinguishing between topics that specifically discuss a word versus those that only mention it.
Participant A agreed that ranking would be very useful for single terms.
Participant B suggested that for multiple terms, a simple approach could be used instead of ranking.
Participant A proposed that for multiple terms, the system could disregard pairs that do not show up together or apply a negative weighting against them.
Participant B confirmed that if terms do not appear together, they would not show up in the search results.
Participant C agreed to disregard search results where terms do not appear together.
The group decided not to implement a start-up window for the search feature at this time.
Participant C stated they would write up the meeting summary and send it to Pernilla.
